messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ethan was seven the first time his father’s hand landed on his back, a blow that sent him sprawling onto the cold bedroom floor. It happened at night, after his father had been drinking, the only sounds the dull thud of fists and the sharp cry of his younger sister from the next room. Ethan learned to brace himself against the rough wool of his father’s sweater—a texture he would later feel under his own fingers whenever the memory returned. The abuse continued for years, always in the dark, always with his sister’s wailing in the background. He had no way to escape.

In the years since, Ethan carried the belief that others could see what had been done to him just by looking at his face—a shameful exposure that made his skin crawl. He felt like an object, something used and discarded, and he became certain that anyone, anywhere, could harm him without warning. This constant sense of vulnerability meant that any hint of darkness or a child’s cry felt like a direct threat, a trigger that yanked him back into that bedroom. The night sky outside his window, the coarse fabric of a towel at work, a toddler fussing in a supermarket aisle—each one flooded his mind with the full sensory weight of the original event: the smell of his father’s breath, the sting of the wool, the sound of his own sobs muffled against the floor. The memory did not just return; it overwhelmed him, playing like a film he could not stop, forcing him to stop whatever he was doing until the wave passed.

To survive, Ethan developed a set of habits that made sense to him but steadily shrank his world. Whenever a trigger hit, he would abandon whatever he was doing—dropping a mop mid-sweep, walking out of a client’s house, quitting a job rather than risk another night shift. He learned to make sure he was never alone with another person, because being alone felt like being cornered, an invitation to be hurt again. And when the memory became unbearable, he would drift off into a fantasy world inside his head, a safe place where he was invisible and untouchable. The memory itself would often push him into these escapes: the film would start, and he would mentally disappear. But the escape had a cost—the act of drifting sometimes seemed to summon the memory even more vividly, as if his mind punished him for trying to hide. And each time he dropped a responsibility or avoided a person, he confirmed his deepest appraisals: he was not a real person anymore, just a broken object that others could see right through.

Ethan also experienced sudden flashbacks—moments when he felt as if his father were still in the room, his body tensing, heart racing, palms slick with sweat. He remained hypervigilant, always scanning for the wrong texture, the wrong sound, the wrong shift in light. These felt like facts of his life, not something he could connect to anything else.

Now twenty-five, Ethan works as a housekeeper in a small hotel. He only takes day shifts, avoiding the darkness that would wait for him at dusk. He cannot touch certain rough fabrics without his stomach turning. He has lost two previous cleaning jobs because he walked out mid-shift or failed to show up after a trigger. He is deeply isolated and single. What finally brought him to seek help was a morning when a child in a nearby room began crying; he dropped his cleaning cart in the hallway and fled to the stairwell, where he stood shaking for twenty minutes. His manager gave him a final warning. Ethan is terrified that he will lose this job too, and more than that, he is terrified that the memory will never stop coming. He hopes someone can teach him how to make it go away without his whole life falling apart. Each time the film started, he caught himself thinking that he must be fundamentally broken for this to keep happening. And after the film ended, he would find himself scanning the room for anything—textures, sounds, shadows—that might start it again.
